answers.answer: Caching can help because the same few station-language pairs account for most reads and guides change only weekly, so the API otherwise repeats the same database work. A cache keeps a reusable copy of a result. Reading that copy can save database work and shorten the wait for the page. The database takes 80 ms to build a guide and a cache lookup takes 2 ms, so a hit avoids that slower lookup. The database remains the source of truth. In this example, the database owns the product record. Losing the cached copy must not lose the guide. A cache key identifies the result to reuse. English and Spanish guides differ, so the key must include the inputs that change the answer: the station ID and the language. A key such as guide:42:en, distinct from guide:42:es, follows the same pattern as product:42 for shared details and product:42:USD when the answer changes. Reusing one language's guide for another language would return the wrong guide. The application uses cache-aside, so the API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the guide from the database on its own. On a hit, the API finds the station-language key in the cache and returns its stored guide. A hit avoids this database lookup. On a miss, the entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the guide. The API is who reads the database and who stores the cached result. A miss still needs the database, so the 80 ms build remains. Before a copy exists, the API still does the database lookup. Storing that copy uses memory and adds a cache write. The cache adds a lookup on the read path and a write when the copy is stored.

answers.answer: Reader C receives the old hours. Reader A missed, read the old hours from the database, and paused. Writer B then committed the new hours and deleted the cache key. Reader A resumed and stored the old hours it already fetched. Reader C looks up the key before it expires and hits that refilled entry, so C receives the old hours. Deletion failed to prevent that because saving the new hours and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch the old value before the update, pause, then refill the old value after removal. The next cache hit still returns the old hours. Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. The team cannot claim that every read after B finishes sees the new hours. Reader C's lookup happens after B finishes and still returns the old hours. If this endpoint must always show the latest committed hours, validate the hours against the authoritative database instead of serving this stale cached copy. A database commit makes the completed write available to subsequent database reads, so reading the database for the response avoids returning the old copy Reader A wrote back. That does not require a concurrency protocol.

Remove the cached entry after saving the new price in the database. A later miss reloads it.
Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. To avoid charging an old price at checkout, validate the price against the authoritative data as part of accepting the order.
Removal can also fail.
A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.

answers.answer: The forecast stored at 12:00 keeps the original cached value until that entry expires or is removed. There is no background refresh and no write-triggered invalidation, so the source change at 12:02 does not replace the cached forecast. A TTL sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. The ten-minute TTL promises only that lifetime: the entry may remain until 12:10. It does not promise that the cached forecast matches the source, and it does not refresh the forecast when the source changes. A TTL does not refresh the data on a timer; a later miss must load it again. TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it. In case A the entry stays in memory until it expires. The request at 12:03 can use the original cached forecast, because the entry is still present and a hit returns the stored value even when that value is old. The request at 12:11 must fetch the source. The ten-minute TTL has expired, expired entries are not served, and a later miss must load the forecast again. In case B the cache removes the entry at 12:04 to free memory, and the request at 12:05 must fetch the source because the entry is absent. That memory removal is eviction, a different event from TTL expiry. Eviction removes entries to make room, and an entry can be evicted before its TTL ends. The ten-minute TTL would still have allowed the entry to remain at 12:05; the removal happened to free memory, not because the TTL elapsed.

answers.answer: A shared cache is the simpler fit for the goal that one cache deletion removes the cached map used by every instance. Today each of the four instances keeps an independent local cache. A local cache lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. One can hold the old map while another holds the new map. When an organizer changes the map, the database updates and only the instance handling that write deletes its local copy. Requests sent to the other instances still use those instances' own copies, so those requests can still receive the old map. A shared cache puts the map in one separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached, that the four API servers share. With a single shared entry, deleting that one key removes the copy every instance uses. The team can accept the 2 ms network lookup. Local lookups happen inside each API process and avoid a network call. Shared lookups happen at that separate cache service, and each lookup adds a network call. One cost of the shared cache is that the service needs operating. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries. Losing one local cache is narrower: restarting one API process discards its local cache, and other processes keep their copies. Losing cache access does not by itself establish whether the application requests fail. Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database, so the writer still deletes the shared key after the database update.

answers.answer: The endpoint receives 10,000 requests per second, mostly for the same schedule, and the database can safely handle only 500 schedule reads per second. The cache normally absorbs almost all reads. When the popular key expires while many requests arrive together, those requests miss together. Many requests miss the same schedule and repeat its database lookup. That stampede can send far more than 500 reads per second to the database. Coalesce the concurrent misses so those readers share one in-progress lookup. One request reads the database and the others wait for that same result instead of each starting another schedule read, which removes the duplicate database reads from that burst. When the entire cache is unreachable for a minute, the application cannot read a value from a cache it cannot reach. A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Sending all 10,000 requests per second to the database would overwhelm the 500 reads per second it can handle. Do not send every request straight to the database. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle and reject excess requests. The product permits a temporary error to protect the database, so requests beyond the database's capacity can fail instead of all becoming schedule reads. The product also permits the last known schedule for up to 60 seconds, but a stale copy can be used only when it remains reachable outside the failed cache, such as a response the process still holds. Serve older data only where the product rules permit it and a copy remains reachable outside that failed cache, such as a response the process still holds. That response reduces work because coalescing turns many duplicate lookups into one shared database read, and during the outage only a limited number of requests reach the database while excess requests are rejected or answered from a copy the process still holds. Falling back to the database is a load decision, not a free recovery path.

Serve older data only where the product rules permit it and a copy remains reachable outside that failed cache, such as a response the process still holds.

answers.answer: The team should not add this cache now. Every result has a unique ID and each result is retrieved exactly once before archival, so a later request does not reuse the stored copy. The expected benefit is about none. If requests rarely reuse results, the cache may cost more than it saves. Before a copy exists, the API still does the database lookup, and that 2 ms read is the only read of the result. A hit never avoids a repeated lookup that does not occur. The costs are a cache write after every database read, memory for a copy that is not read again, and another copy to manage. The endpoint already has a 100 ms latency budget and the database read takes 2 ms. Ten reads per second is well within the 1,000 reads per second the database can handle, so the cache is not relieving latency or capacity. Reconsider if the workload changes so the same inspection results are read many times before archival. Repeated reads of the same ID would be work worth avoiding, and a cache hit could then save database work and shorten the wait.
